title: Amendment 4: Gubernatorial Term Limit

context.text: Referred to the ballot by the Louisiana Legislature as House Bill 225 (Act 414), sponsored by Rep. Mike Bayham (R-Chalmette). It needs two-thirds of each chamber and no gubernatorial signature. The Louisiana Illuminator reported that two earlier House floor attempts fell three votes short of the two-thirds mark before it passed; the bill history shows the Senate passed it 28-10. The Illuminator described the House vote as falling mostly along party lines.

question.text: Do you support an amendment to prohibit a person who has served more than one and one-half terms as governor from being elected as governor for any future term? (Amends Article IV, Section 3(B))

summary.text: Current law provides that a person who has served as governor for more than one and one-half terms in two consecutive terms cannot be elected governor for the succeeding term. The amendment removes the consecutive-terms language, so a person who has served more than one and one-half terms as governor could not be elected governor again at any future time. The Louisiana Illuminator reported that it would also prevent a governor re-elected in 2027 from seeking a third term. No fiscal note was posted with the bill.

measure.yesMeans: Changes the governor's term limit from a bar on a third consecutive term to a lifetime bar: someone who has served more than one and one-half terms as governor could not be elected governor again.
measure.noMeans: Keeps current law, which bars only a succeeding (consecutive) term for someone who has served more than one and one-half terms in two consecutive terms.

argumentsFor.text: Rep. Mike Bayham (R-Chalmette), the sponsor, said after the House vote, as reported by Louisiana Radio Network: “I believe that it’s healthy that we have a change of perspective and new blood in one of the most powerful executive positions in the United States.” The Louisiana Illuminator reported that Bayham said he supports term limits for other statewide offices but considers them a priority for the governor because of the office's power (paraphrase).

argumentsAgainst.text: Rep. Mark Wright (R-Covington), who voted against the bill, said in a text message after the vote: “The author said publicly that it was about preventing John Bel Edwards from becoming governor again,” and “If we were really worried about incumbents abusing power, we would include all the other statewide offices where we've seen incumbents abuse power as much as governor.”

researchNotes: Ballot question text is the proposition printed in the enrolled joint resolution, which directs that it be placed on the Nov 3, 2026 ballot; vote counts, Act numbers and fiscal information are from the Louisiana Legislature's bill pages, résumé digests and Legislative Fiscal Office notes. The Louisiana Secretary of State's certified list could not be loaded (sos.la.gov election pages returned 404 on Oct 19, 2026), so the Amendment 1-10 numbering and the question wording were checked against the nonpartisan PAR Guide to the Fall 2026 Constitutional Amendments, which lists the same ten amendments in the same order with the same question text; the parenthetical effective-date and constitutional-citation text follows the enrolled resolution. Louisiana has no citizen initiative and publishes no voter-pamphlet arguments; a majority of votes cast approves an amendment. Bayham's quoted words are from Louisiana Radio Network; the Illuminator's description of his reasoning is a paraphrase by that outlet. The Illuminator reported a 74-23 House vote on May 5; the bill history shows 73-25 for that roll call, so the official history is used here only for the Senate vote.
